Hi Vanessa + Sergio,

Thanks again for taking the time last week. We pulled together a short patterns doc that shows three deployment models we commonly deploy with ISV partners: 1) cold S3 + local pgvector primary, 2) managed hot-cache (partner) + cold object store, and 3) unified managed vector DB with an edge read-replica for latency-sensitive reads. The attached PDF is the patterns overview and includes rough cost sensitivity (hot vs cold) and where we typically recommend doing model-quantization vs retrieval-layer caching.

A few quick notes:
- We typically see best cost/latency with a small hot cache (P99 < 120ms) and S3-backed cold tier for long-tail vectors.
- For customers with strict tenancy needs, we push a partner-hosted hot cache in a dedicated VPC and use signed S3 URLs for cold fetches.

We'd love to run a 6-week pilot for one of your mutual customers where VectorWave runs the hot cache and Redwood provides the inference + routing policy. Attached: vectorwave-embedding-patterns.pdf (2 pages).

Would you be open to a quick sync to sketch a mutual action plan?

Vanessa — quick technical readout after reviewing Amit's patterns doc. TL;DR: feasible with three recommended configuration patterns, with tradeoffs clearly called out.

Pattern A — Local primary (pgvector) + S3 cold fallthrough
- Behavior: local pgvector hosts fullable index for recent/top-k; misses routed to S3 cold retrieval + remote re-embedding (if necessary).
- Pros: simple infra (self-hosted), lowest inter-provider network egress.
- Cons: heavier RAM/disk footprint on customer infra; cold fetchs spike tail latency.
- Ops estimate: ~40–60 dev/eng hours to add routing + prefix/KV caching; infra cost depends on node counts.

Pattern B — Partner-hosted hot cache (VectorWave) + Redwood inference + S3 cold tier
- Behavior: Redwood routes nearest requests to partner hot cache; partner responds with vector IDs and scores, Redwood hits model only for generation when necessary. Fallback to S3 when cache miss.
- Pros: offloads memory & scaling to partner; predictable hot latency (they can tune lane sizes).
- Cons: cross-account auth, network hops, must validate SLA and data retention.
- Ops estimate: ~20–30 dev/eng hours to implement routing hooks + auth (mTLS + signed urls).

Pattern C — Fully-managed vector DB (partner or vendor) + read replica in edge region
- Behavior: partner runs full vector DB; Redwood maintains lightweight read-replicas for latency-critical routes.
- Pros: low dev effort on our end for index ops; best tail latency if replicas are close to reads.
- Cons: commercial complexity; replication consistency and cold-tiering policy required.
- Ops estimate: ~30–50 dev/eng hours (depends on replica automation).

Security notes:
- We must require per-customer encryption keys and audit logging for partner-hosted caches. Recommend requiring KMS-backed keys and an initial SOC2 questionnaire before pilot sign-off.

Recommendation for pilot: start with Pattern B (partner-hosted hot cache) because it demonstrates the routing layer and commercial split while minimizing customer infra setup. Dev effort modest (~25h) and we can measure latency delta quickly.

I can draft a short technical appendix with endpoint specs, auth header samples, and caching TTLs if folks want to hand it to VectorWave before the sync.

—Dev Patel
